column1: Trees can share nutrients underground
column2: Fungal networks link the roots of many trees in a forest. Through them, trees can exchange water, carbon and nutrients, though how much and why is still debated.
column3: Forests are more connected than they look.

column1: Sloths can hold their breath longer than dolphins
column2: By slowing their heart rate, sloths can hold their breath for up to about 40 minutes. Dolphins usually surface every 8 to 10 minutes.

column1: Flamingos are pink because of their food
column2: Flamingos are born grey. Pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat turn their feathers pink over time.
column3: You really are what you eat.

column1: A group of crows is called a murder
column2: The term dates back to the 15th century, when groups of animals were given poetic names. A group of owls is a parliament.

column1: Cows have best friends
column2: Studies found cows show lower stress when paired with a preferred companion. They form close social bonds within herds.
column3: Social needs run deep across species.

column1: Bamboo can grow almost a metre a day
column2: Some bamboo species can grow up to about 90 centimetres in a single day. It is one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
column3: Growth rates can be astonishing when conditions suit.

column1: Sea otters hold hands while sleeping
column2: Sea otters often float in groups called rafts and sometimes link paws so they do not drift apart. They also wrap themselves in kelp.
column3: Simple habits can solve hard problems.

column1: Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day
column2: Eucalyptus leaves are low in nutrients and hard to digest. Koalas save energy by sleeping most of the day.

column1: Some jellyfish can reverse ageing
column2: Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to an earlier life stage when stressed. In theory this cycle could repeat indefinitely.
column3: Nature bends rules we think are fixed.

column1: Elephants can recognise themselves in a mirror
column2: Asian elephants have passed the mirror test, touching marks on their heads they could only see in a reflection. Few animals pass it.
column3: Self-awareness is not unique to humans.

column1: Owls cannot move their eyes
column2: Owl eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets. Instead, owls can turn their heads around 270 degrees.

column1: Bees communicate with a dance
column2: Honeybees perform a waggle dance to tell others the direction and distance of food. The angle of the dance points relative to the Sun.

column1: Hummingbirds cannot walk
column2: Their feet are tiny and suited for perching, so they shuffle or fly even short distances. Their wings can beat dozens of times a second.

column1: Penguins propose with pebbles
column2: Male gentoo penguins search for smooth pebbles to offer females. Pebbles are used to build nests that keep eggs off cold ground.
column3: Courtship often has a practical side.

column1: Tardigrades can survive in space
column2: These tiny animals, under a millimetre long, survived exposure to the vacuum of space in a 2007 experiment. They can dry out and revive years later.
column3: Toughness comes in very small packages.

column1: Crocodiles cannot stick out their tongues
column2: A membrane holds a crocodile's tongue to the roof of its mouth. It helps stop water flowing into the throat when it opens its jaws underwater.

column1: The Amazon makes much of its own rain
column2: Trees release huge amounts of water vapour through their leaves. This moisture forms clouds and rain over the forest and beyond.
column3: Ecosystems can create their own weather.

column1: Seahorse fathers give birth
column2: Female seahorses lay eggs in a pouch on the male, who carries them until they hatch. He then releases fully formed young.
column3: Parenting roles vary widely in nature.

column1: Garden snails have thousands of teeth
column2: A snail's tongue-like radula is covered in rows of tiny teeth, often numbering in the thousands. It scrapes food like a rasp, and worn teeth are replaced.
column3: Small creatures can carry surprising tools.

column1: Wombats leave cube-shaped droppings
column2: Uneven stiffness in a wombat's intestine shapes its droppings into cubes. They use them to mark territory on rocks and logs.
column3: Even odd details have a mechanism.

column1: Giraffes have the same number of neck bones as you
column2: Giraffes and humans both have seven neck vertebrae. Each of a giraffe's can be over 25 centimetres long.

column1: Dolphins have names
column2: Bottlenose dolphins develop signature whistles that work like names. Others use them to call specific individuals.

column1: Mushrooms are closer to animals than plants
column2: Genetic studies show fungi share a more recent common ancestor with animals than with plants. Like us, they cannot make food from sunlight.

column1: Snails can sleep for years
column2: In dry conditions, some snails seal themselves in their shells and go dormant. They can stay that way for months, occasionally years.
column3: Waiting can be a survival skill.

column1: Butterflies taste with their feet
column2: Butterflies have taste receptors on their feet. Landing on a leaf tells a female whether it suits her caterpillars.
column3: Senses can be placed where they are most useful.

column1: Polar bears have black skin
column2: Under their white-looking fur, polar bears have black skin that absorbs heat. Their fur is actually transparent and hollow.
column3: Things are not always the colour they seem.

column1: A woodpecker's tongue wraps around its skull
column2: The tongue extends from the back of the mouth, around the skull, and helps cushion the brain from impact.

column1: Some sharks must keep swimming to breathe
column2: Species like the great white rely on water flowing over their gills as they swim. Others can pump water while resting.
column3: Not all sharks follow the same rule.

column1: Arctic terns make the longest migrations
column2: Arctic terns fly between the Arctic and Antarctic each year. Over a lifetime they may travel a distance equal to going to the Moon and back several times.
column3: Small birds can be extreme travellers.

column1: Pigeons are smarter than their reputation
column2: Experiments suggest pigeons can learn to distinguish images and even recognise objects in pictures. They are smarter than their reputation.

column1: Squirrels forget where they bury many nuts
column2: Squirrels bury far more nuts than they eat. Forgotten ones can grow into new trees.

column1: Rats laugh when tickled
column2: Researchers found rats make high-pitched chirps when tickled, which some interpret as a form of laughter.
column3: Joy may be more widespread than we think.

column1: A snail can sleep while stuck to a wall
column2: Snails rest in cycles, sometimes clinging to surfaces with dried mucus. They can stay attached for long periods.

column1: Kangaroos cannot walk backwards easily
column2: Their large tails and powerful legs make backward movement very awkward. They are built to bound forward.

column1: Starfish can regrow arms
column2: Many starfish can regenerate lost arms. Some species can grow a whole new body from one arm if it contains part of the centre.

column1: Hippos produce a reddish secretion
column2: Hippos release an oily red fluid that acts like sunscreen and may protect against germs. It is sometimes called blood sweat but is neither.

column1: Leaves change colour as green fades
column2: In autumn trees break down green chlorophyll. Yellow and orange pigments that were there all along show through.
column3: Some colours are always present, just hidden.

column1: Elephants have a sensitive trunk
column2: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles and can pick up a single peanut or lift heavy logs.

column1: Honeybees visit millions of flowers for a jar of honey
column2: Making a single jar of honey can take bees around two million flower visits.
column3: Small efforts add up to sweet results.

column1: Male lions sleep up to 20 hours a day
column2: Lions save energy by resting most of the day. Hunting is short and intense.
column3: Rest is part of the strategy.

column1: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals
column2: Coral polyps build hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Over thousands of years, they create reefs.
column3: Tiny builders can make huge structures.

column1: Some birds use tools
column2: New Caledonian crows shape twigs and leaves into hooks to pull insects from holes.
column3: Tool use is not unique to humans.

column1: Moles can dig fast
column2: A mole can dig several metres of tunnel in an hour. Its front paws are broad and powerful like shovels.
column3: Bodies are tools for a lifestyle.

column1: Pandas spend most of the day eating
column2: Giant pandas eat bamboo for around 10 to 16 hours a day. Bamboo is low in nutrients, so they need a lot.

column1: Earthworms improve soil
column2: Earthworms mix soil and leave nutrient-rich casts. Charles Darwin spent years studying their importance.
column3: Small creatures can have big impacts.

column1: Some fish can climb waterfalls
column2: Certain Hawaiian gobies use suction-cup fins to climb high waterfalls to reach upstream habitats.

column1: Deer grow new antlers each year
column2: Male deer shed their antlers annually and grow a new set. Growing antler is among the fastest-growing animal tissue.
column3: Renewal can be built into life cycles.

column1: The largest living thing may be a fungus
column2: A honey fungus in Oregon spreads underground across nearly 10 square kilometres. It may be thousands of years old.
column3: The biggest things can be hidden.

column1: Bats are the only mammals that truly fly
column2: Some mammals glide, but bats are the only ones capable of powered flight. Their wings are stretched skin over long fingers.

column1: Chameleons change colour mainly to communicate
column2: Colour changes often signal mood or territory rather than camouflage. They also help with temperature control.
column3: The obvious explanation is not always right.

column1: Ducks have waterproof feathers
column2: Ducks spread oil from a gland near their tails over their feathers. Tightly interlocking feathers also help keep water out.

column1: Some plants can sense touch
column2: The sensitive plant Mimosa pudica folds its leaves when touched. It may deter grazing animals.
column3: Plants are more responsive than they seem.

column1: Owls fly almost silently
column2: Special feather edges break up turbulence, letting owls approach prey with very little sound.

column1: Goldfish have better memories than the myth
column2: The "three-second memory" is a myth. Studies show goldfish can remember things for months.

column1: Pigs are very intelligent
column2: Pigs can learn tricks, solve puzzles and recognise individuals. Some studies compare them to dogs.

column1: Zebras' stripes may deter flies
column2: Research suggests stripes confuse biting flies, making them less likely to land.

column1: A blue whale calf gains around 90 kilograms a day
column2: Blue whale calves drink rich milk and grow very fast in their first months.
column3: Growth can be astonishing early on.

column1: Spider silk is extremely strong for its weight
column2: Some spider silk is stronger than steel of the same thickness and very stretchy.

column1: Some trees communicate danger with chemicals
column2: When attacked by insects, some trees release chemicals that may prompt nearby trees to boost their defences.

column1: Axolotls can regrow limbs
column2: These Mexican salamanders can regenerate limbs, parts of the heart and even parts of the brain.

column1: Frogs drink through their skin
column2: Most frogs absorb water through a patch of skin on their belly rather than drinking with their mouths.

column1: Peacock feathers get their colour from structure
column2: The shimmering colours come from microscopic structures that reflect light, not pigments.
column3: Colour can be built, not dyed.

column1: Sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched
column2: Female sea turtles often return to nest near where they were born, possibly guided by Earth's magnetic field.

column1: Camels store fat, not water, in their humps
column2: The hump stores fat for energy. Camels survive without water by conserving it efficiently.
column3: Myths often get the mechanism wrong.

column1: Horses cannot vomit
column2: A strong muscle at the entrance to a horse's stomach makes vomiting nearly impossible.

column1: The mantis shrimp packs a fast punch
column2: Its club-like limbs strike so fast they create bubbles that collapse with tiny shock waves. It can crack shells and glass.

column1: Crows can hold grudges
column2: Studies found crows remember faces of people who threatened them and warn others.

column1: Bees can recognise human faces, some studies suggest
column2: Experiments indicate honeybees can learn to tell apart images of faces.
column3: Even tiny brains can learn patterns.

column1: Dragonflies are expert hunters
column2: Dragonflies catch a very high share of prey they chase, among the most successful hunters known.

column1: Flamingos stand on one leg to save energy
column2: Studies suggest standing on one leg takes less muscle effort for flamingos and may reduce heat loss.

column1: Male emperor penguins incubate eggs
column2: Males balance eggs on their feet under a fold of skin through the Antarctic winter, fasting for weeks.

column1: Some caterpillars mimic snakes
column2: Certain caterpillars have markings that look like snake eyes, scaring off birds.

column1: Orcas are dolphins
column2: Killer whales are the largest members of the dolphin family. They live in complex social groups.

column1: Grass grows from the base
column2: Grass grows from near the ground, not the tips. That is why it survives grazing and mowing.
column3: Where you grow from determines how you recover.

column1: Raccoons wash food, or seem to
column2: Raccoons often dunk food in water. Scientists think it may heighten their sense of touch rather than clean it.

column1: Hummingbirds can fly backwards
column2: Their wings rotate at the shoulder, letting them hover and fly in any direction, including backwards.

column1: Sunflowers follow the Sun when young
column2: Young sunflowers track the Sun from east to west. Mature flowers usually face east.

column1: Cuttlefish can change texture as well as colour
column2: They can alter skin colour and surface texture in moments to blend into surroundings.

column1: The platypus lays eggs
column2: The platypus is one of the few mammals that lays eggs. It also detects prey using electrical signals.

column1: Some ants farm fungus
column2: Leafcutter ants cut leaves to feed fungus gardens, which they then eat. They have farmed for millions of years.

column1: Rainforests cover a small share of land
column2: Tropical rainforests cover around 6 percent of Earth's land but hold a large share of its species.
column3: Small areas can hold great riches.

column1: Koalas have fingerprints like humans
column2: Koala fingerprints are so similar to ours that they can be hard to tell apart under a microscope.

column1: Some octopuses use coconut shells as shelter
column2: Veined octopuses carry coconut halves and assemble them into shelters when needed.
column3: Planning ahead is not unique to us.

column1: Snakes smell with their tongues
column2: A snake flicks its tongue to collect scent particles and passes them to an organ in the roof of its mouth.
